someone asked me why, with my physics undergrad background and a PhD in economics, I had decided to become a professional blogger. I told him that blogging seemed like the highest-leverage thing I could do, in terms of actually having an impact on the world. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I didn’t mean that bloggers literally rule the world, of course — this isn’t </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/21160ab1-dc62-41b9-a4bb-edfd3f6cb34f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Ender’s Game</a></em><span>. Nor do I have any illusions that I’ll be able to have as much influence as a top politician like Donald Trump, a top entrepreneur like Elon Musk, and so on. But in terms of what </span><em>I could personally accomplish</em><span>, it seemed like a no-brainer — being an opinion writer has probably allowed me to change the world much more than being an academic or an engineer or a financier or a consultant would have. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why? Because blogging has allowed me to </span><em>inject ideas into the discourse</em><span> with unparalleled speed, breadth, and access. A researcher goes deep into a few topics; a blogger can quickly hit the main points of many topics. This enables </span><em>speed</em><span>; academics might take months to write something useful about a breaking event like the Iran War or Trump’s tariffs, while I can have something out in hours. It also enables me to comment on a wide variety of topics, because people expect me to be an analyst rather than a subject-matter expert. And speed and breadth in turn allow me to talk to a wide variety of important and interesting people — top academics, billionaire company founders, presidential advisors. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Injecting ideas into the discourse is incredibly powerful. John Maynard Keynes famously described the power of idea injection:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Practical men, who believe themselves to be quite exempt from any intellectual influences, are usually the slaves of some defunct economist. Madmen in authority, who hear voices in the air, are distilling their frenzy from some academic scribbler of a few years back.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To describe </span><em>why</em><span> idea injection is so powerful would take an entire post (which I do intend to write). There are a number of reasons. First, idea injection allows you to </span><em>frame the terms of the debate</em><span>. Whether people think your idea is right or wrong, once you put it out there, discussion of the issue at hand turns into discussion of whether your idea is good or bad. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As Keynes notes, an early writer’s ideas can also act as a kind of training data for later thinkers; it becomes a foundation off of which politicians, bureaucrats, staffers, other writers, and even entrepreneurs and financiers build when they make their own ideas.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">¹</span><span> Just today I saw </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d5a45700-33ed-4723-bb8d-c24410b270e4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Matt Yglesias and Jerusalem Demsas</a><span> — two of my favorite pundits — riffing on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d497bd99-6d3a-410d-ba5b-3c112c592b18?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">my post on dating advice</a><span> on their podcast.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But injecting ideas is only one part of a blogger’s influence. We’re also part of a community of intellectuals that span multiple disciplines and walks of life. On a daily basis I get to mull ideas over not just with other writers and pundits, but also with top academics, CEOs and entrepreneurs, Congressional staffers and political advisers, think-tankers, corporate researchers and engineers, and plenty of people from other countries. This leads to a much richer discussion, with a greater diversity of viewpoints, than almost anything else I can think of. And they reach a very wide set of ears. In a way, blogging is like DARPA — ad-hoc multidisciplinary teams that build the rapid prototype of an idea. OK, maybe that’s a bit pretentious, but you get the point. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Anyway, the reason I’m writing all of this is not to brag, but to complain. Over the last two years, I’ve felt like my job has become a bit less important than it used to be, for three reasons:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The rise of populism on all sides of the political spectrum in the U.S. means that smart ideas are simply not as likely to be implemented by the people in power.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The general shift to Substack and other monetizable direct-to-audience channels has made punditry less conversational.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The rapid proliferation of AI writing has increased the demands on readers’ attention (including my own).</p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This doesn’t mean I think punditry is dead or unimportant — despite the title of this post, I </span><em>do </em><span>think that what I write still matters — but it does mean I’m now spending some time thinking about how to regain some of the impact I felt I had a couple of years ago.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Populism means being intellectual is a liability</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>“Thus when the irreverent intellectual has done his work…The stage is now set for the fanatics.” — Eric Hoffer</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ten years ago, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f02752f0-a346-4050-ad70-6466dd0c740f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">it was already apparent</a><span> that wonkish policy types were to have a much diminished role under Donald Trump. Trump himself is not the type of person who’s inclined to listen to egghead intellectuals — he’ll always trust his own instincts, which were usually developed watching CNN in the early 1990s. In his first term, though, he could sometimes be prevailed upon to listen to reason when a crisis struck — Operation Warp Speed and the CARES Act were done under his auspices, because he stepped back and allowed smarter folks to take over. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And in Trump’s first term, it still felt like there were lots of relevant ideas for econ types to debate — trade policy, place-based economic policies, new socialist ideas from the Bernie camp, and so on. It felt like a time of great political ferment and upheaval — even if Trump himself wasn’t listening to economists, someone would be soon. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In Trump’s second administration, though, that’s all gone. Whether it was Covid, Trump’s advancing age, or his attempted overthrow of the 2020 election that made Trump totally lose faith in everyone but himself, the big man now seems inclined to listen only to the voices in his own head. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Take tariffs, for instance. Essentially no one thought — or thinks now — that his tariffs were a good idea. Oren Cass, one of the last few tariff defenders, has been reduced to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e2ece281-ce37-4a65-b0a2-ee6420063d38?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">speaking in snarky generalities</a><span> about how “econ isn’t a science”, because on some level he knows that the way Trump went about imposing tariffs is intellectually indefensible. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/803e8d7d-d353-46cc-9652-8588090712e8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Peter Navarro</a><span>, of course, at least until he got sidelined. But Trump didn’t get the tariff idea from Navarro. He thought of it all himself, and then looked around for someone — anyone! — who would be willing to stand in front of a podium and endorse the policy, and Navarro was just the guy he found. Reading Peter Navarro’s books, or trying to start a dialogue with Navarro, would have been useless, because Navarro’s ideas — such as they are — weren’t actually driving anything. It was all just a cult of personality.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The rest of Trump’s administration is the same way. The “MAHA” antivax insanity, the research funding cuts, the doomed war in Iran, the reckless spending — it’s all just ad-hoc stuff that Trump did, either on a whim, or because the last guy he talked with told him it would be a good idea, or because he’s in damage control mode after a drop in the S&P. There’s no </span><em>intellectual</em><span> movement here, just a cult of personality. There’s no one to argue with, because nothing that’s happening is based on an argument in the first place.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This state of affairs will eventually end, of course. Whoever succeeds Trump won’t have his cult of personality, and will </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/812661cb-601b-4108-82db-612a6e840325?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">have to rely on ideologies</a><span> and ideas that will be ripe for debate. And if a Democrat retakes the White House in 2028, ideas will be back on the table, as they were during the Biden administration. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But even on the left, the trend is away from open intellectual debate. Zohran Mamdani and the other socialist candidates who are winning primary races in blue cities are interested in ideas, but only from people within their own clique. Leftism in America is fundamentally a </span><em>factional</em><span> movement disguised as an ideological one; bloggers who aren’t on the team will simply be ignored, except for the occasional denunciation. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is just </span><em>populism</em><span>. Populism isn’t really about doing stuff that’s </span><em>popular</em><span>; it’s about putting factional and tribal conflict above the national interest or the general public good. The goal is always to “own” the other side, and economic and social outcomes become subordinate to that goal. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Intellectualism thrives in times of relative social peace. This isn’t one of those. Hopefully, the tide of populism is receding in America, but the experiences of other countries suggest that these times of factional struggle can go on for a very long time. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Monetization means intellectuals are siloed</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>“Writing is like prostitution. First you do it for love, and then for a few close friends, and then for money.” — Ferenc Molnár</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Substack has done a whole lot of good, both for me personally and (more importantly) for the world. In a time when </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3751e23a-1ba2-4d46-96a8-90f43957a33d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">most of the internet has been taken over</a><span> by malignant opportunists and sensationalist attention-seekers, Substack stands as a lone island where reasoned, intelligent, earnest debate is still possible. It has also allowed many writers to escape from publications that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7151d4c7-b73f-4feb-89ea-840f4483c94c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">stifle their voice, impede their development</a><span>, and don’t pay them their due. In many ways, Substack has resurrected the old blogosphere from the early 2010s. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, this resurrection has come at a price. Substack’s killer feature — email distribution — allows writers to get much larger and more loyal audiences, and to make a lot more money by charging those audiences for subscriptions. But this creates a financial incentive for writers to spend more time serving their customers and </span><em>less time talking to each other</em><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In 2011, I was blogging part-time, because it was fun — the attention that mattered was when Brad DeLong or Paul Krugman or Tyler Cowen was interested in something I had to say. It was a little “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/30776796-4820-4656-ac28-f342ff3f3f33?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">republic of letters</a><span>”. Now I’m blogging full-time, and having a conversation with Brad or Paul or Tyler is still just as fun and stimulating, but it’s a distraction from my job of creating content for my paying audience. There are still </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6dcf870e-1617-402c-b86e-cefa79160d1f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">interesting intellectual debates and exchanges</a><span> in the blogosphere, but they are no longer the main thing writers are </span><em>rewarded </em><span>for. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Turning intellectuals into content creators tends to put them in siloes. And Substack is far from the strongest in terms of silo-ing. Most of the internet is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/080a25fe-39be-49ee-8b1c-62c228e2ed4a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">being taken over by vertical-scrolling short-form video</a><span>, which is not exactly good for conversation and exchange. I could go start a YouTube channel, but it would just be me talking directly to my fans — I’d basically be a TV talk show host. I might still do this, because it’s a high-leverage way to influence the world, but it’s not as intellectually rich or rewarding as being part of a round-table conversation. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Nor are interesting new ideas as likely to emerge from one-way siloed content creation. Ideas emerge not from singular minds in isolation, but from dialogue — the cross-pollination that the blogosphere and other intellectual communities create isn’t just fun, it’s productive. Writing for you, my readers, is not </span><em>boring</em><span>, but you’d get better content from me — and from all your other favorite writers — if we talked to each other more.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I do think that platform companies could consciously try to recreate intellectual dialogue by tweaking the features of their platforms. Substack has tried to do this with the Substack Live feature, with modest success. But a more powerful tool would be to allow Substackers to easily and automatically see when another Substacker links to their blog. This feature existed on Blogger in 2006 — whenever another website linked to you, you’d see how many pageviews it drove to your blog. If Substack implemented this feature, it would get a lot of writers talking to each other more often. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">AI is stretching our attention to the breaking point</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>“My ambitions accelerate. My afternoons do not.” — Claude</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Unlike </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a4052fc5-0492-4508-b928-e3d56e4ae100?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">many people</a><span>, I think AI writing is actually pretty good. Yes, there’s a recognizable style that the basic models use (“It’s not X, it’s Y” and lots of other little cliches). That style isn’t bad, it just gets overplayed when everyone uses it.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">²</span><span> Yes, AI models are still not great at boiling a complex idea down to one or two pithy sentences. But you can </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/82cecd4a-c015-47e6-8703-f85c19d36425?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">modify the style that AI uses</a><span>. And AI can do plenty of things human writers can’t — it can seamlessly incorporate vast knowledge and novel data analysis into a piece as it writes it. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, I immediately suspected that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d6f2e4b6-a559-410f-bf6d-e5cfdebd55a1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">this essay</a><span> by Aaron Brown, Michael Mendelson, and Cliff Asness, on the confusion of the debate over “affordability”, is mostly AI-generated, and Pangram — the most reliable AI text detector — flagged it as around 50% AI. But that’s not a knock against it — </span><em>the essay is great</em><span>. It classifies different kinds of “affordability” problems — true poverty, precarity, downward mobility, etc. — into different buckets, gives some illustrative vignettes, and provides some useful numbers about each one. I broadly agree with the article’s conclusions, and I think it’s a valuable addition to the discourse. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A bigger problem is that in a world where a huge number of people generate effectively infinite amounts of good-quality content like this, it becomes hard for readers to decide where to allocate their attention. Instead of identifying the few most consistently useful blogs and reading those in great detail, a lot of people will respond to the explosion of content by “reading” a larger number of posts but only lightly skimming each one. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s not my job I’m worried about here. It’s that in that world, even if my blog continues to get tons of readers and make me plenty of money, what I do becomes less important. If people are just skimming what I write so they can move on to the next 10,000-word Claude-generated post, the fact that they’re paying me $10 a month is cold comfort — I’m not really reaching them. And even more worryingly, </span><em>no one</em><span> is reaching them — if they’re skimming 100 posts a day instead of reading 10 all the way through, they’re not getting really good information from </span><em>anywhere</em><span>.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">³</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I don’t know how severe this problem will be, to be honest. There was always a lot more high-quality content on the internet than anyone could ever read, and a lot of people always just skimmed my posts instead of reading them closely. Maybe AI </span><em>can’t </em><span>make this problem worse because it was already maximally bad. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also, I’m optimistic that AI itself will open up new channels for intellectual influence. It’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b81821d8-5985-4892-b5a1-16b7929ea404?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a well-known fact</a><span> that if AI just consumes AI-generated output, it gets worse and worse. So AI companies try very hard to “clean” the text they use to train their models. Human writers, whose personal experience brings in new data for AIs to learn, can influence the world if their writings are used to train the next generation of AIs. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Interestingly, I think I’m already doing this, quite by accident. I don’t know how reliable the website </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1cffe6de-7a31-42af-bf9b-152be2822d13?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" This is the third such payment by the Trump administration to undo offshore wind projects that have been years in the planning. Trump has so far committed $2.5 billion in taxpayer dollars to killing renewable energy projects. The administration has also tried to stop offshore wind farms already under development — moves that have been blocked by the courts — while the Pentagon has been refusing to grant routine permits for onshore wind projects.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Yes, $2.5 billion to destroy already-approved, cost-effective clean energy projects while Americans are suffering from soaring electricity prices thanks to data centers and high gasoline prices.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Yet here’s the irony: Donald Trump’s disastrous Iran war has delivered a huge boost for renewable energy around the world — except in the U.S.. Trump has so far done more to shift the global economy away from fossil fuels and towards renewable energy than any other single individual in history.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Why do Trump and his gang hate green energy so much? The roots of their hatred range from the power of fossil fuel interests, to Trump’s petulant whine that wind turbines ruined the view from his Scottish golf course, to a general sense among right-wingers that clean energy threatens their masculinity.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What’s best for Americans has nothing to do with it. Thus, Trump lackeys justifying their hostility to renewables consistently make arguments even they must know are stupid. Consider, for example, an </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d49e6996-8c80-4cfe-ae99-0cadb95da3b9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">exchange</a><span> last month between Doug Burgum, secretary of the interior, and Rep. Jared Huffman of Nevada:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>Burgum</em><span>: All of these projects you’re describing in Nevada have one thing in common—when the sun goes down, they produce zero electricity.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>Huffman</em><span>: Mr. Chairman, I request unanimous consent to enter in the record this amazing new technology that apparently the secretary is unaware of: It’s a battery.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Indeed. To get a clearer understanding of far battery technology has progressed in enabling the transition to renewables, let’s look at how the state of California sourced its electricity this past Wednesday. The chart below shows megawatts supplied at 15-minute intervals over the course of the day. The area shaded yellow represents daylight hours. The light blue line at the top is electricity generated by renewables, mainly solar power (with some wind and hydro as well). In addition to supplying energy for current consumption, renewables supply energy to batteries for nighttime consumption. The black line at the bottom is net electricity supply from batteries — which is negative when batteries are charging, positive when they’re being drawn down:</p><div underline;">more than half</a><span> of its electricity from renewables. It is rapidly becoming a state largely powered by the sun during daylight hours and powered by batteries during the night.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Burgum’s suggestion that solar is an unproven or unreliable technology is completely at odds with reality.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Nor is California the only economy that now makes substantial use of renewable energy. Burgum’s home state of North Dakota gets more than a third of its electricity from wind power (don’t tell Trump). In South Dakota wind supplies 57 percent of the electricity. And renewables generate a large share of electricity in many countries, including most big European economies. (France is the outlier, not because it relies on fossil fuels, but because it has large nuclear capacity.) Spain, for example, now relies heavily on a solar-plus-batteries system similar to that in California.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And when Trump went to war with Iran, nations that had already shifted toward renewable energy were very glad they had made the move.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To the extent that there’s a competition for the future of electricity generation, it’s between renewable energy and natural gas. Whatever Trump may want to believe, burning coal — even ignoring the environmental damage — is a costly, obsolete technology, which nobody wants to invest in. But new gas-turbine power facilities are still being built (although many places are, like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b145c8c2-f9c8-497f-a158-5e434db4e716?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">California</a><span>, rapidly </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a70dffff-8f0d-412c-be8a-b078e4c287e2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">shifting away</a><span> from natural gas). Trump officials envision a world largely powered by US liquefied natural gas (LNG).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, countries that relied heavily on natural gas were hit hard by Trump’s gratuitous war with Iran. LNG supplies from the Persian Gulf were blocked and couldn’t be fully replaced by U.S. exports because shipping capacity was limited. Countries that had invested heavily in renewables, like Spain, were largely unscathed. A </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/13c5bf5d-2896-4a35-9233-2a6a69db7b81?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">report</a><span> from the think tank Ember found that since the war began Spanish electricity prices — unlike prices in some other European countries — were essentially decoupled from the soaring price of natural gas.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Assuming that the Strait of Hormuz will be reopened after Trump’s abject surrender to the Iranian regime, natural gas prices should subside. Yet the world has learned a hard lesson about the riskiness of relying on fossil fuels for electricity generation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And let’s be clear about the nature of that lesson. It’s not the fact that much of the world’s supply of hydrocarbons comes from a politically volatile region: We’ve known that all too well since the 1970s. What’s new is the recognition of American weakness and unreliability.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In this new era of drone warfare America cannot guarantee reliable access to imported fossil fuels through critical sea lanes. And is America itself a reliable supplier? Can nations that allow themselves to be dependent on U.S. gas and oil be sure that Trump or a future Trump-like president won’t weaponize that dependence, cutting off or threatening to cut off supplies in some future dispute? The obvious answer is no.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The whole world now knows that relying on imported fossil fuels is a major economic and security risk. By contrast, the sun will shine and the wind blow whatever may be happening overseas. Renewables were already rapidly becoming cheaper than fossil fuels. Now it’s clear that they are also far safer.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Thus Donald Trump has in practice become the world’s green energy champion.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">MUSICAL CODA</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/6e3ea218-a2ba-4aef-a886-ed4b7c356ec6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="margin-bottom: 0;display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/KQetemT1sWc" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>Because Japan did this later than other rich nations, immigrants aren’t yet as numerous as in Europe or the U.S., but the percentage is rising fast. And so discussions about what it truly means to be Japanese are starting to emerge.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>I thought it would be useful for my readers — most of whom live in America or other English-speaking nations that are going through their own crises of national identity right now — to get some perspective on how Japanese people think about these issues. And so I asked my friend Hiroko Yoda to write me a post about it. </span><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Hiroko is a Japan-based entrepreneur, cultural historian, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2aba616b-5e71-4862-a8a9-db8c6af4e930?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><span>writer</span></a><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">. She's the author of a new book, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b630cce0-ce10-4f59-abe7-e4716d8c7827?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><span>Eight Million Ways to Happiness</span></a><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">, which is a memoir exploring Japan's modern secular-spiritual landscape. She also writes </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aeef6fac-c95f-47a8-ab98-b6e9a5a458ac?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><span>on Substack</span></a><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">In this post, she writes about how shared culture, rather than adherence to a particular religious doctrine, is what binds Japan so tightly together. Interestingly, “culture” is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dc64ed29-f51e-4a88-adaf-35bc7f5c43d0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">the same answer I arrived at</span></a><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> when I asked the question of what will bind America together in the future. </span></em></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Although I live in Japan, as a Japanese person married to an American, and who studied at American universities for my undergrad and graduate degrees, I probably pay more attention to happenings in the U.S. than many Japanese people. One of the topics I have found most interesting is the ongoing struggle to define what an American is. The reason being, we Japanese are grappling with this issue as well.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e7f6812d-6b39-4434-9d30-df48c649f3f9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><span>As Noah has written</span></a><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">, Japan is accepting more immigrants than ever before. When my husband and I moved to Tokyo in 2003, international couples were still uncommon, and we’d sometimes draw stares if we walked hand in hand. These days, it’s completely unremarkable. The numbers of tourists visiting Japan increase year by year, and so does the number of people taking permanent residence. I see many international families in the suburb where we live, and I don’t think we are unusual, at least as regards urban centers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">As Japanese are finding new ways to co-exist and live alongside non-Japanese, they are also revisiting what it means to be Japanese. As</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/73f6daeb-569b-4ee9-82d1-10edd99c6311?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><span> I’ve written</span></a><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> in my own newsletter, the question once centered simply on ethnicity, but now many are coming to believe that shared cultural values are more important.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Are you Japanese simply because of where you were born, or are you Japanese because of how you participate in society? Superficially, this resembles the arguments going on in America. Are you American because of some kind of heritage, or are you American because you embrace shared values, like those laid out in the Constitution?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">But there is an interesting difference, too. Japan is (or was) a country with relatively little immigration; that’s why the question of who’s Japanese traditionally hinges on ethnicity. On the other hand in America, an immigrant melting pot, the litmus test often seems to return to faith.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">It comes up again and again in American discussions about what it means to be American. Take this recent essay from </span><em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">The New York Times</span></em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> opinion writer Ross Douthat:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">One doesn’t need to be a specific </span><em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">kind </span></em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">of religious believer to be a good believer in the Declaration [of Independence]. But if you look at the sweep of American history, it’s very hard to disentangle the advance of equality from the religious belief that our rights come from God and that human beings are equal in his eyes… it has more power in a context where most Americans believe in a providential God.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">And then there’s Derek Thompson, who in a recent conversation with religious scholar Ryan Burge, noted:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">There’s this category of Americans who have gone into religion as if it’s a foreign country, harvested certain souvenirs, and brought them back to the world of secularism. They practice yoga but have no interest in understanding its religious origins. They meditate but are not remotely interested in any Buddhist version of nirvana.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">To which Burge replies:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">They only wanted the parts of religion they liked and left the others behind…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">You can’t just pick and choose…A lot of people are doing that with religion right now. They’re walking down the buffet line, picking one piece, putting it on their plate, and calling it a spiritual life. That doesn’t endure.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">And Thompson concludes:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">If you don’t have that central spine of purpose, the community won’t last. If your only purpose is “let’s get together,” that’s not enough. You need that higher purpose—that vertical spine—in order to build a truly strong horizontal community.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">These pundits are arguing that ideas alone – the values of the Declaration of Independence or the Constitution – aren’t enough to keep Americans together, whether in communities or as a country. America’s loneliness epidemic, its polarization, its young citizens’ loss of hope: a big part of it can be attributed to the fact Americans don’t go to church or synagogue or temple or what have you anymore.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">All of which makes me want to say: have you ever been to Japan?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Japanese, as a nation, don’t subscribe to any one faith. In fact, there’s a popular saying “born Shinto, married Christian, buried Buddhist.” We pick and choose, bringing what we like from various traditions – the purifications of Shinto, the pretty aspects of Christian weddings, the traditions of Buddhist funeral rites – into our secular lives. We’re so flexible about it that we often answer no when people ask if we’re religious. Look at this chart:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">I’m going to put aside the question of how accurate this is. I actually wrote an </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b630cce0-ce10-4f59-abe7-e4716d8c7827?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><span>entire book</span></a><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> on how I believe surveys like this can miss the forest for the trees. (Spoiler: it involves how one defines “religion.”) But Burge and others argue Americans are “setting themselves up for failure” in becoming less religious, or at least in not going to religious institutions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">America is a flexible society that is rigid when it comes to religion; Japan is the opposite, a rigid society with a surprising flexibility when it comes to faith. There’s an old phrase that sums up Japan’s traditional spiritual cosmology: </span><em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">yaoyorozu no kami</span></em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">, which means eight million deities. It isn’t an accounting; it’s an expression of awe at the infinite nature of the sublime in all its forms. It incorporates, absorbs, rather than draws lines. In short, it’s radically inclusive.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">I get that America is a religious country. I was taken to Sunday school every week when I was a homestay student in Indiana in the 1990s. I recited the Pledge of Allegiance alongside the other students every day. But there’s no pledge of allegiance in Japanese schools. The Japanese flag wasn’t even displayed in any of my classrooms. None of my classmates ever went to anything resembling a Sunday school.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">But we were united in other ways. Ways that look like faith to outsiders, but just felt like everyday life to us. We made New Year’s visits to shrines or temples for </span><em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">hatsumode</span></em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">, a first prayer for the year. Many of us had Buddhist-style altars in our homes, where we kept photos of departed family members. Many of us carried </span><em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">omamori</span></em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">, Shinto or Buddhist amulets for scholarship or travel safety on our schoolbags.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">But if you’d asked the majority of us what our faith was, or who we were praying to, we’d have reacted with utter confusion. None of us saw amulets as a replacement for studying, or looking both ways before crossing the street. They were simply cute ways to wish. If you’d asked us what we </span><em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">believed</span></em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">, I honestly don’t think we would have even understood the question. We just </span><em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">did</span></em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">So if institutional faith is core to the communities that form a healthy society, why is Japan’s so successful without it?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">First, let me be clear here. I don’t see Japan as some kind of utopia or even a role model. I just see it as different. But the fact it is different – and not struggling in the ways many commentators seem to think America is struggling, at least regards faith as an identity – is what might make the Japanese counterpoint relevant. Let me also be clear that I believe faith can nurture a life or a community. If your personal faith nourishes you, I cheer you on.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">But speaking broadly, if Japan can maintain a stable society without faith, it would seem to indicate it isn’t a </span><em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">necessity</span></em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> for a healthy society.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">So what </span><em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">is</span></em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> keeping Japan together?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">For a long time, Japanese could rely on clear lines to define themselves, like language (Japanese being little spoken outside the nation) and terrain (being an archipelago). But things are changing, and changing fast. It isn’t particularly difficult to get to Japan anymore. More people outside Japan are learning and speaking Japanese than ever before. More want to live here than ever before.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">And Japan is aging and shrinking. We’ve “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8336adc0-4049-4552-a05f-e2bc7a65a701?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><span>lost</span></a><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">” three million citizens over the last few years alone, as deaths outpace births. The numbers of foreign visitors and permanent residents are higher than ever before. All of these factors are driving the question of what it means to be Japanese, which is playing out in online forums, TV shows, newspapers, and election contests throughout Japan.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">A </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/770e7245-9c7f-4c86-9960-0136f0e4faca?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><span>recent Stanford survey</span></a><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> about immigration shows that race isn’t a major factor in resistance to immigration. Rather, Japanese language ability is. In this chart, you can see how many more respondents chose to admit a hypothetical immigration applicant based on their ability to speak fluently.</span></p><div 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Now, this might seem like a no-brainer. Of course, you want to admit people who can communicate with you. But “fluent” is doing a lot of lifting here that might not be obvious in English.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Japanese is classified as a “high-context” culture, meaning that a large amount of cultural knowledge is required to speak fluently. (Other high-context cultures include China, Korea, and many Arab countries.) There’s a lot of implicit communication, meaning context is often implied rather than expressed directly. Meanwhile, Americans, Germans, and Scandinavians (among others) are framed as “low-context,” meaning conversations tend to be explicit, with context usually spelled out.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Anyone who’s studied Japanese will know what I mean. We often leave pronouns and even subjects out, in casual speech. You’re expected to </span><em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">kuuki wo yomu</span></em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> – “read the air” and intuit meaning. So when Japanese say they want immigrants to master Japanese, they’re talking less about the linguistics of speaking than they are context – “the air,” in other words.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">In a recent </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a9e43351-90dc-49aa-8f90-f5cb90b9d69a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><span>survey</span></a><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">, 62% of Japanese reported that they wanted immigrants to not only follow the rules, but also “etiquette and customs.” Some interpret this as draconian or authoritarian, but I don’t think so. If you correlate it with that Stanford survey, you can see that once Japanese fluency is achieved, locals ranked people of a wide variety of ethnic backgrounds as acceptable (the dot at far right in each graph.)</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Of course, not everyone in Japan agrees with this thinking. There are those who have a vested interest in keeping the definition of Japanese as strict as possible, who use foreigners as scapegoats for society’s failings, who wish to keep the number of outsiders who immigrate here as low as possible. The </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/003c581b-ba5d-44be-b5cc-0b746bd01e57?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><span>far-right party</span></a><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> that rode an anti-immigrant platform to a surprising number of seats in parliament in the 2025 elections is one example. But I believe the winds are against people who think in this way. The demographics are against them. The technologies that let us cross borders physically, and share our ideas across them virtually, are against them. And most of all, I think our cultural traditions are against them. When our cosmology, so to speak, is so inclusive, it’s hard to square why our society should not be. Anyone who trumpets conservative values in Japan is eventually going to run up against that conundrum.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">As a Japanese, it isn’t my place to say who is or isn’t an American. But I can say what I personally envision for my country’s identity going forward. I see it in little moments all over the city today. Non-Japanese employees greeting customers in polite Japanese. Foreign folks showing respect at temples and shrines. The caucasian man and his daughter I saw commuting to kindergarten on a </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/93c44a22-945e-48d2-bc96-af2a75dbf99b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><span>mama-chari</span></a></em><span data-color="rgb(0, 0, 0)" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);"> bike, her tiny pastel backpack slung incongruously over his big shoulders. In other words, the stuff of everyday life. To me Japanese isn’t what you look like; it’s how you act. In other words, it’s how you read the air.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border:
